newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Morocco to vote in local poll with eye on parliament.
newsitem.headline: Morocco to vote in local poll with eye on parliament.

text.p: More than 100,000 Moroccans wind up campaigning on Thursday for seats on local councils which later this year will play a key role in selecting a new Upper House of Parliament.

More than 13 million voters are eligible to cast their ballots on Friday to elect 1,547 local councils which King Hassan wants to have a greater say in running the country, both locally and through the yet-to-be-created second tier of parliament.

"The importance of Friday's polls reside in the fact that future communal repesentatives will hold 3/5th of the upper house," Mohamed El Yazghi, a leading figure of the opposition Socialist Union of Peoples Forces, said.
The remaining third will be elected indirectly through trade unions, chamber of commerce and industry bodies before the end of September, officials said.

Morocco's present one-chamber, 333-seat assembly is to become a two-house parliament after legislative elections for the lower house in September. The lower house will be directly elected by universal suffrage. The new upper house will have power to topple the government by a no-confidence vote supported by an absolute majority of its members.

For more than three decades pro-government parties dominated parliament while the opposition was marginalised because of lack of confidence between the palace and opposition leadership, said a Western diplomat.
Now, according to Ali Yata, leader of the opposition Progress and Socialism Party (PPS), "the (expected) alternating democratic process starts on June 13 (local election day)".
Yata was referring to King Hassan's vision of a multi-party system, in which he sketched out "two alternating political blocs in power, with a strong group in the centre to create a balance".
Morocco's dozen parties roughly reflect this picture.

The four main opposition parties, grouped in a bloc known as the Koutla Addimocratia (democratic bloc), are fielding a total of 33,987 candidates. The parties are the Istiqlal, USFP, PPS and the Organisation of Democratic and Popular Action (OADP).
The Wifaq (consensus) group of rightwing parties has 24,079 candidates. They come from the Constitutional Union (UC), the Popular Movement (MP) and the National Democratic Party (PND).
The third group, in theory representing the centre, groups the Rassemblement National des Independants (RNI), Social and Democratic Movement and Popular National Movement (MNP) parties.

Last year King Hassan told the nation of 28 million people in a televised speech: "I am fed up with people saying that Morocco's elections were not fair or manipulated...I assure you that I will put my personal weight and constitutional powers to ensure that the (future) elections will be honest and transparent."

After the 1993 legislative elections, the opposition, which gained 125 seats out of the total 333, declined a royal invitation to join the government because it said "the election results did not reflect the true political map of the country due to the administration's manipulations."
The Koutla had 21.3 percent of seats in communal elections of 1992 while pro-government and centre-right took up to 65 percent, an official at the interior ministry said.

"First indications are that the 1997 elections will be relatively transparent and fair...Morocco is sending a clear message abroad which says the opposition can legally take over power if it wins voters' support," the Western diplomat said.
